Inputs and initialization

Source: vignettes/articles/inputs.Rmd
inputs.Rmd

Scaling, neighborhood construction, and initialization can change an embedding as much as the choice of cost function. smallvis exposes these choices so that you can hold them fixed while comparing methods. This guide covers the current interface; the linked experiments explore their effects.

Choose the input representation

Supply a numeric matrix, a data frame, or an R dist object. Rows are observations and columns are features; nonnumeric columns of a data frame are filtered out. Use a dist object for precomputed distances: an ordinary square matrix is still treated as observations and features.

set.seed(42)
distance_fit <- smallvis(
  dist(iris[, 1:4]),
  scale = FALSE,
  Y_init = "rand",
  perplexity = 30,
  epoch_callback = FALSE,
  n_threads = 1,
  verbose = FALSE
)
dim(distance_fit)
## [1] 150   2

Feature scaling and PCA need the original features, so choose those before calculating distances. PCA initialization also needs features; random or suitable spectral initialization can be used with distance inputs.

Scale and reduce the features

The default scale = "absmax" applies one global rescaling. Use scale = TRUE to center and scale each feature, or scale = FALSE to retain its original units. The input scaling experiment illustrates why these choices matter.

Input PCA is separate from PCA initialization. With pca = TRUE, initial_dims controls how many input components are retained before affinities are calculated. Here the four iris features are reduced to three:

pca_fit <- smallvis(
  iris,
  scale = TRUE,
  pca = TRUE,
  initial_dims = 3,
  Y_init = "spca",
  perplexity = 30,
  ret_extra = "X",
  epoch_callback = FALSE,
  n_threads = 1,
  verbose = FALSE
)
dim(pca_fit$X)
## [1] 150   3

Use pca = "whiten" to additionally give the retained components unit variance. Whitening changes the relative importance of components, so it changes the distances used by the embedding. See the PCA and whitening experiments before treating it as a routine speed optimization.

Set the neighborhood size

For Gaussian affinities, perplexity controls the effective neighborhood size and must lie between 1 and the number of observations minus 1. Try a few values when exploring a dataset; changing perplexity changes the affinities being fitted, so final costs at different perplexities are not a common score for selecting the best picture.

For UMAP’s smoothed-neighbor affinities, the same argument controls neighborhood size rather than Gaussian perplexity. The function reference gives its precise meaning for each input choice.

See perplexity, intrinsic dimensionality, and multiscale perplexities for experiments with alternatives to a single global setting. The supported forms are documented in the intrinsic dimensionality and multiscale reference sections.

Choose the starting coordinates

The default Y_init = "rand" draws a small random Gaussian layout. Set the random seed immediately before the call when you want to repeat a run in the same environment. Y_init = "spca" starts from scaled PCA scores, avoiding the variation from random starting coordinates. These are different uses of PCA: pca changes the input distances; Y_init changes where optimization begins.

Y_init = "laplacian" and Y_init = "normlaplacian" use spectral coordinates from the input graph. They need a suitable affinity matrix. The optional RSpectra package accelerates these initializations; without it, smallvis uses base R’s full eigendecomposition. You can also pass an explicit matrix with one row per observation and one column per output dimension to Y_init.

The initialization experiments compare starting layouts, and Spectral Methods explains the different graph constructions and eigenvectors. For repeated random starts, continue to optimization and repeated runs.
